claim: Transgenic rats expressing cre-recombinase under the tyrosine hydroxylase (TH) promoter were stereotactically injected with cre-dependent virus containing the inhibitory DREADD hM4Di (Experimental, n = 4) or mCherry-only control (Control, n = 3) into bilateral VTA.
source: Transgenic rats expressing cre-recombinase under the tyrosine hydroxylase (TH) promoter were stereotactically injected with cre-dependent virus containing the inhibitory DREADD hM4Di (Experimental, n = 4) or mCherry-only control (Control, n = 3) into bilateral VTA (Figure 1A).
evidence: This is a direct statement about the experimental procedure performed, describing the animal model, viral injection, and group sizes.

claim: Widespread expression across the extent of VTA and co-localization with TH was observed.
source: We observed widespread expression across the extent of VTA and co-localization with TH (Figure 1B, Figure 1—figure supplement 1), enabling specific and reversible inactivation of VTA dopamine signaling.
evidence: This claim is supported by histological data shown in Figure 1B and Figure 1—figure supplement 1, demonstrating viral expression patterns.

claim: Post-experiment histology confirmed overlapping virus expression and TH-positive neurons in putative VTA near the injection site (–5.6 mm AP from bregma), as well as approximately 0.5 mm anterior and posterior (−5 to –6 mm AP).
source: Post-experiment histology confirmed overlapping virus expression and TH-positive neurons in putative VTA near the injection site (–5.6 mm AP from bregma), as well as approximately 0.5 mm anterior and posterior (−5 to –6 mm AP).
evidence: This is a direct statement about histological findings confirming the anatomical location of viral expression.

claim: Tetrodes were lowered to the pyramidal cell layer of dCA1, using the presence of SWR with upward deflections in the LFP, recording depth characteristic of dCA1, and spatially restricted firing of place cells to confirm the recording location.
source: Tetrodes were lowered to the pyramidal cell layer of dCA1, using the presence of SWR with upward deflections in the LFP, recording depth characteristic of dCA1, and spatially restricted firing of place cells to confirm the recording location.
evidence: This describes the methodology used to confirm the recording location in the hippocampus.

claim: The duration of Unch. reward end stopping periods decreased from Epoch 1 to Epoch 2.
source: (G) The duration of Unch. reward end stopping periods decreased from Epoch 1 to Epoch 2. The mean stopping durations in each condition were calculated per session, then analyses performed across sessions. Mean ± standard error, Exp Saline, Epoch 1: 6.67 ± 0.61, Epoch 2: 5.13 ± 0.53; Exp CNO, Epoch 1: 7.766 ± 0.61, Epoch 2: 6.04 ± 0.42. Con Saline, Epoch 1: 6.96 ± 0.4, Epoch 2: 4.77 ± 0.27; Con CNO, Epoch 1: 6.59 ± 0.29, Epoch 2: 4.43 ± 0.15. Mixed-effects generalized linear model (GLM) with epoch, drug, animal group, and all interactions, with individual animal as a random effect: epoch, z = −3.37, p < 0.001; all other terms, n.s.
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis of behavioral data showing significant epoch effect.

claim: The duration of Incr. reward end stopping periods increased from Epoch 1 to Epoch 2.
source: (I) The duration of Incr. reward end stopping periods increased from Epoch 1 to Epoch 2. The mean stopping durations in each condition were calculated per session, then analyses performed across sessions. Mean ± standard error, Exp Saline, Epoch 1: 6.64 ± 0.54, Epoch 2: 10.87 ± 0.8; Exp CNO, Epoch 1: 7.28 ± 0.66, Epoch 2: 12.31 ± 0.82. Con Saline, Epoch 1: 7.44 ± 0.78, Epoch 2: 11.29 ± 0.5; Con CNO, Epoch 1: 6.47 ± 0.35, Epoch 2: 10.34 ± 0.27. Mixed-effects GLM with epoch, drug, animal group, and all interactions, with individual animal as a random effect: epoch, z = 4.62, p < 10–5; all other terms, n.s.
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis of behavioral data showing significant epoch effect.

claim: VTA inactivation did not prevent rats from recognizing a devalued location.
source: Though visit durations were slightly longer in CNO sessions in experimental rats, particularly in novel track sessions, this behavioral effect of a relative value decrease remained, indicating VTA inactivation did not prevent rats from recognizing a devalued location.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the behavioral data showing that despite VTA inactivation, rats still showed behavioral signatures of recognizing value changes.

claim: In experimental rats, CNO and reward both influenced SWR rate, with significant effects for the CNO main effect (z = 3.19, p < 0.01), the interaction between Incr. end and Epoch 2 (z = 9.02, p < 10–10) and the three-way interaction between Incr. end, Epoch 2, and CNO (z = −2.06, p < 0.05).
source: In experimental rats, CNO and reward both influenced SWR rate, with significant effects for the CNO main effect (z = 3.19, p < 0.01), the interaction between Incr. end and Epoch 2 (z = 9.02, p < 10–10) and the three-way interaction between Incr. end, Epoch 2, and CNO (z = −2.06, p < 0.05).
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis using a Poisson GLM on SWR rate data.

claim: Control animals showed no apparent effect of CNO on SWR rate.
source: Control animals showed no apparent effect of CNO (Figure 2C). The same Poisson GLM fit to control rat data confirmed this, with significant coefficients only for Incr. end (z = −2.42, p < 0.05) and the interaction between Incr. end and Epoch 2 (z = 7.64, p < 10–10).
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis showing no CNO effect in control animals.

claim: SWR duration was reduced in novel sessions, consistent with replays becoming longer with increased familiarity.
source: SWR duration was reduced in novel sessions, consistent with replays becoming longer with increased familiarity (Berners-Lee et al., 2021), as well as in Epoch 2, but was otherwise unaffected by reward or drug (Figure 2—figure supplement 4).
evidence: This claim is supported by data analysis and is consistent with previous findings cited.

claim: The actual difference in SWR rates between saline and CNO sessions in experimental animals during Epoch 2 was significantly greater than chance in novel sessions for both the Unch. end (one-tailed test, CNO > saline, p < 0.001) and the Incr. end (one-tailed test, saline > CNO, p < 0.01), as well as at the Unch. end in familiar sessions (one-tailed test, CNO > saline, p < 0.01).
source: We found the actual difference in SWR rates between saline and CNO sessions in experimental animals during Epoch 2 was significantly greater than chance (Figure 2—figure supplement 1A) in novel sessions for both the Unch. end (one-tailed test, CNO > saline, p < 0.001) and the Incr. end (one-tailed test, saline > CNO, p < 0.01), as well as at the Unch. end in familiar sessions (one-tailed test, CNO > saline, p < 0.01).
evidence: This claim is supported by bootstrap statistical analysis comparing actual data to shuffled controls.

claim: There was no significant difference between saline and CNO in control animals at either reward end in either familiar or novel sessions.
source: There was no significant difference between saline and CNO in control animals at either reward end in either familiar or novel sessions (Figure 2—figure supplement 1B; one-tailed tests, all n.s.).
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis showing no effect of CNO in control animals.

claim: Across both familiar and novel environments, CNO reduced the difference in SWR rate between the Incr. end and Unch. end in experimental rats but not in control rats.
source: Across both familiar and novel environments, CNO reduced the difference in SWR rate between the Incr. end and Unch. end in experimental rats but not in control rats (Figure 2D, E, left panels; experimental group, full mixed-effects model with drug terms strongly outperformed reduced model lacking drug terms, AICreduced–AICfull = 5.22; control group, reduced model lacking drug terms strongly outperformed the full model, AICreduced–AICfull = −3.54).
evidence: This claim is supported by model comparison statistics showing drug effects in experimental but not control animals.

claim: The effect of CNO remained in experimental rats when omitting the first and last 1 s of each stopping period to isolate the reward consumption period.
source: To control for the possibility that VTA inactivation caused changes in locomotor or other non-consummatory behavior at reward wells that might affect SWR emission, we omitted the first and last 1 s of each stopping period to isolate the reward consumption period. The effect of CNO remained in experimental rats, reducing SWR rate discrimination between Incr. and Unch. ends (Figure 2D, E, right panels; experimental group, full mixed-effects model with drug terms strongly outperformed reduced model lacking drug terms, AICreduced–AICfull = 4.55; control group, reduced model lacking drug terms strongly outperformed the full model, AICreduced–AICfull = −3.1).
evidence: This claim is supported by additional analysis controlling for potential confounds.

claim: In all time windows and conditions except novel CNO sessions in experimental rats, the SWR rate at the Incr. end was significantly greater than at the Unch. end.
source: In all time windows and conditions except novel CNO sessions in experimental rats, the SWR rate at the Incr. end was significantly greater than at the Unch. end (Figure 2F, G; Incr. – Unch. significantly greater than 0, one-sample t-test, p < 0.05, uncorrected for multiple comparisons).
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis of SWR rates across different conditions.

claim: In novel sessions, VTA inactivation did not prevent an initially larger increase in SWR rate at the Incr. end than the Unch. end, but caused that difference to diminish over laps.
source: In novel sessions, VTA inactivation did not prevent an initially larger increase in SWR rate at the Incr. end than the Unch. end, but caused that difference to diminish over laps (Figure 2F).
evidence: This claim is supported by analysis of within-epoch dynamics of SWR rate changes.

claim: By the middle of the epoch, there was no statistically significant difference in reward modulation between the reward ends in novel CNO sessions in experimental rats.
source: By the middle of the epoch, there was no statistically significant difference in reward modulation between the reward ends (one-sample t-test, p > 0.05, for 5-lap windows centered on laps 8–13 and 15), consistent with an initial appropriately localized reaction to reward change that eventually spread across the track.
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis of SWR rate differences across laps.

claim: VTA inactivation spared the capacity for increased reward to modulate SWR rate but led to decreased differentiation of low and high value locations, particularly in novel environments where SWR rate increased spatially indiscriminately.
source: Overall, VTA inactivation spared the capacity for increased reward to modulate SWR rate but led to decreased differentiation of low and high value locations, particularly in novel environments where SWR rate increased spatially indiscriminately.
evidence: This is a summary statement integrating multiple findings from the SWR rate analysis.

claim: The mean-subtracted SWR rate was modestly negatively correlated with the previous volume in experimental rats.
source: The mean-subtracted SWR rate was modestly negatively correlated with the previous volume (Pearson correlation: saline, r = −0.076, p = 0.177; CNO, r = −0.109, p < 0.05).
evidence: This claim is supported by correlation analysis of SWR rate and previous reward volume.

claim: A GLM found the mean-subtracted SWR rate was significantly affected by previous volume (z = −2.3, p < 0.05), but not drug (z = −0.24, p = 0.81) or current volume (z = 0.196, p = 0.844).
source: A GLM found the mean-subtracted SWR rate was significantly affected by previous volume (z = −2.3, p < 0.05), but not drug (z = −0.24, p = 0.81) or current volume (z = 0.196, p = 0.844).
evidence: This claim is supported by GLM statistical analysis.

claim: SWR rates were higher for a given current reward volume when the recent reward history was low.
source: SWR rates were higher for a given current reward volume when the recent reward history was low (Figure 3D, E, bottom panels).
evidence: This claim is supported by analysis of SWR rates as a function of reward history.

claim: A Poisson GLM predicting SWR rate as a function of current volume, drug condition, and whether reward history was low or high revealed significant effects of current volume (z = 13.86, p < 10–10) and reward history split (z = −2.23, p < 0.05), but not drug condition (z = −1.05, p = 0.29).
source: A Poisson GLM predicting SWR rate as a function of current volume, drug condition, and whether reward history was low or high (relative to the median for the session) revealed significant effects of current volume (z = 13.86, p < 10–10), as expected, and reward history split (z = −2.23, p < 0.05), but not drug condition (z = −1.05, p = 0.29).
evidence: This claim is supported by GLM statistical analysis.

claim: Mean-subtracted SWR rate was significantly affected by RPE sign (two-way ANOVA with drug and RPE sign, RPE sign: F[1,518] = 6.42, p < 0.05), but not drug (F[1,518] = 0.3, p = 0.582).
source: Finally, we separated combinations of current and previous volume into those with negative RPE (current < previous) and positive RPE (current > previous) and found mean-subtracted SWR rate was significantly affected by RPE sign (Figure 3F; two-way ANOVA with drug and RPE sign, RPE sign: F[1,518] = 6.42, p < 0.05), but not drug (F[1,518] = 0.3, p = 0.582; drug × RPE sign, F[1,518] = 0.07, p = 0.785).
evidence: This claim is supported by ANOVA statistical analysis.

claim: SWR rate was modulated by reward volume changes consistent with RPE-like coding.
source: Taken together, SWR rate was modulated by reward volume changes consistent with RPE-like coding.
evidence: This is a summary statement integrating findings from the volatile reward experiment.

claim: This modulation did not require normal VTA dopamine signaling, at least in familiar environments.
source: This modulation did not require normal VTA dopamine signaling, at least in familiar environments.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the lack of drug effect in the volatile reward experiment.

claim: Place cells in dCA1 had directional fields, such that the location a neuron was active while the rat moved in one direction on the track was often distinct from its activity when the rat moved in the other direction.
source: As previously observed (e.g., Ambrose et al., 2016), place cells in dCA1 had directional fields, such that the location a neuron was active while the rat moved in one direction on the track (e.g., 'upward') was often distinct from its activity when the rat moved in the other direction (e.g., 'downward').
evidence: This claim is supported by observation of place cell firing patterns and is consistent with previous work.

claim: This directionality was apparent in both familiar and novel sessions, including in experimental rats with either saline or CNO.
source: This directionality was apparent in both familiar and novel sessions, including in experimental rats with either saline or CNO (Figure 4A).
evidence: This claim is supported by analysis of place field properties across conditions.

claim: There was no effect of CNO on within-session field reliability, but significantly less reliability in novel compared to familiar sessions.
source: We found no effect of CNO on within-session field reliability, but significantly less reliability in novel compared to familiar sessions (Figure 4—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis of place field reliability.

claim: Field similarity across running directions was slightly but significantly increased by both CNO and novelty.
source: Field similarity across running directions was slightly but significantly increased by both CNO and novelty (Figure 4—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis of place field similarity.

claim: Forward and reverse replays occurred in all conditions, including in novel sessions with saline or CNO.
source: We found forward and reverse replays occurred in all conditions, including in novel sessions with saline (Figure 4B) or CNO (Figure 4C).
evidence: This claim is supported by replay detection and classification across all experimental conditions.

claim: Consistent with previous work, the rate of reverse replay was strongly modulated by the reward volumes on the track.
source: Consistent with previous work (Ambrose et al., 2016), the rate of reverse replay was strongly modulated by the reward volumes on the track.
evidence: This claim is supported by analysis of replay rates and is consistent with previous findings.

claim: In all conditions except novel CNO sessions in experimental rats, when reward was larger at the Incr. end than the Unch. end, reverse replay was significantly increased at the Incr. end relative to when rewards were equal.
source: Excluding novel CNO sessions for the moment, in all other conditions in experimental rats, when reward was larger at the Incr. end than the Unch. end (unequal reward), reverse replay was significantly increased at the Incr. end relative to when rewards were equal (novel saline: equal reward, 0.0019 ± 0.0009 replay/s; unequal reward, 0.0121 ± 0.004 replay/s; two-sample t-test, t(420) = 3.235, p = 0.0013; familiar saline: equal reward, 0.0033 ± 0.0012 replay/s; unequal reward, 0.0128 ± 0.0025 replay/s; two-sample t-test, t(907) = 3.822, p = 0.0001; familiar CNO: equal reward, 0.0033 ± 0.001 replay/s; unequal reward, 0.0139 ± 0.0022 replay/s; two-sample t-test, t(1153) = 5.234, p < 10–6).
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis of reverse replay rates across conditions.

claim: The rate of reverse replay was not significantly increased at the Unch. end with unequal rewards in any of these conditions (all p > 0.05).
source: The rate of reverse replay was not significantly increased at the Unch. end with unequal rewards in any of these conditions (all p > 0.05).
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis showing no significant effect at the unchanged reward end.

claim: In control rats, reward changes caused similar changes to the balance of reverse replay, with a significantly larger swing in reverse replay bias in novel sessions.
source: In control rats, reward changes caused similar changes to the balance of reverse replay (Figure 4H, I), with a significantly larger swing in reverse replay bias in novel sessions (mixed-effects model with drug, novelty, and replay directionality: novelty × directionality, z = 2.18, p < 0.05; all other terms, n.s.).
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis of replay rates in control animals.

claim: Reward changes caused no consistent effects in the rates of forward replay.
source: Reward changes caused no consistent effects in the rates of forward replay (Figure 4F, G and J, K), nor in the rates of replay that began far from the animal (non-local replay, Figure 4—figure supplement 3).
evidence: This claim is supported by analysis showing no significant effects on forward replay rates.

claim: In novel CNO sessions in experimental rats, reverse replay rate failed to be biased toward the larger reward location.
source: Conversely, in novel CNO sessions in experimental rats, reverse replay rate failed to be biased toward the larger reward location (Figure 4D).
evidence: This claim is supported by analysis of replay rates showing lack of spatial bias with VTA inactivation in novel environments.

claim: This effect of VTA inactivation on the bias of replay between the reward ends when reward contingencies changed was specific to novel sessions and reverse replay.
source: This effect of VTA inactivation on the bias of replay between the reward ends when reward contingencies changed was specific to novel sessions and reverse replay (mixed-effects model with drug, novelty, and replay directionality: drug × novelty × directionality, z = −2.27, p < 0.05; novelty, z = −2.01, p < 0.05; novelty × directionality, z = 2.15, p < 0.05; all other terms, n.s).
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis showing specific interaction effects.

claim: VTA dopamine signaling was required to direct reward-related changes in reverse replay, specifically in novel environments.
source: VTA dopamine signaling was therefore required to direct reward-related changes in reverse replay, specifically in novel environments.
evidence: This is a summary statement integrating the replay analysis findings.

claim: VTA dopamine signaling is critical for driving hippocampal SWR and reverse replay selectively to locations with increased reward.
source: Here, we demonstrated a critical role for VTA dopamine signaling in driving hippocampal SWR and reverse replay selectively to locations with increased reward.
evidence: This is a summary of the main finding of the study.

claim: This was true only in novel environments, with only modest effects of VTA inactivation on SWR rates and no discernible effect on replay rates in environments that had been explored several times before.
source: Surprisingly, we found this was true only in novel environments, with only modest effects of VTA inactivation on SWR rates and no discernible effect on replay rates in environments that had been explored several times before.
evidence: This is a summary of the novelty-dependent effects observed in the study.

claim: While SWR rate was modulated by RPE, VTA inactivation had little effect on this RPE-like modulation, suggesting that at least in familiar environments normal VTA dopamine signaling is dispensable for this reward-related hippocampal activity.
source: While SWR rate was modulated by RPE, VTA inactivation had little effect on this RPE-like modulation, suggesting that at least in familiar environments normal VTA dopamine signaling is dispensable for this reward-related hippocampal activity.
evidence: This is a summary statement integrating findings from the volatile reward experiment.

claim: Previous work in other brain areas found hM4Di activation suppressed firing rates to around 60% of baseline.
source: Previous work in other brain areas found hM4Di activation suppressed firing rates to around 60% of baseline (Mahler et al., 2014; Chang et al., 2016), in addition to diminished synaptic transmission even when spikes occurred (Stachniak et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Dopamine neuron firing rates are elevated in novel environments.
source: Dopamine neuron firing rates are elevated in novel environments (McNamara et al., 2014; Takeuchi et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Early in experience dopamine neuron activity ramps while mice run toward both larger and smaller rewards and this ramping activity declines over experience until modest ramps persist only toward the larger reward.
source: More specifically, early in experience dopamine neuron activity ramps while mice run toward both larger and smaller rewards and this ramping activity declines over experience until modest ramps persist only toward the larger reward (Guru et al., 2020).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to a previous study.

claim: Activation of VTA projections to dorsal CA1 improves retention of spatial learning of a novel maze configuration, while also promoting replay-related reactivation.
source: Activation of VTA projections to dorsal CA1 improves retention of spatial learning of a novel maze configuration, while also promoting replay-related reactivation (McNamara et al., 2014), while inactivation of VTA causes an increase in spatial working memory-related errors in novel, but not familiar, environments (Martig et al., 2009).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: LC axons in CA1 are active in locations immediately preceding a new reward location in a familiar environment but not in a novel one, despite similar behavior in both cases indicating mice had learned the reward locations.
source: LC axons in CA1 are active in locations immediately preceding a new reward location in a familiar environment but not in a novel one, despite similar behavior in both cases indicating mice had learned the reward locations (Kaufman et al., 2020).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to a previous study.

claim: LC neurons are modulated by reward-predicting stimuli similarly to substantia nigra dopamine neurons.
source: This result, coupled with findings that LC neurons are modulated by reward-predicting stimuli similarly to substantia nigra dopamine neurons (Bouret et al., 2012; Bouret and Richmond, 2015), suggests LC activity can convey reward-related information and thereby compensate for VTA inactivation, but only in familiar environments where it is not signaling more general novelty.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: VTA can directly or indirectly mediate hippocampal plasticity and spatial learning and memory.
source: Altogether, our work adds to the body of evidence that VTA can directly or indirectly mediate hippocampal plasticity and spatial learning and memory (Gasbarri et al., 1996; McNamara et al., 2014; Rosen et al., 2015; Rossato et al., 2009), and suggests an intriguing distinction between the function of VTA and LC dopamine release in hippocampus (Duszkiewicz et al., 2019).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Reverse replay may provide a neural eligibility trace by which spatial positions can be associated with their proximity to reward.
source: By activating representations associated with the location of the current reward and then progressing sequentially to earlier positions that preceded reward, reverse replay may provide a neural eligibility trace by which spatial positions can be associated with their proximity to reward (Foster and Wilson, 2006; Sutton and Barto, 1998).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous studies and represents a theoretical interpretation.

claim: VTA dopamine neurons are activated when SWR and replay occur during a spatial working memory task, but not during subsequent sleep.
source: Indeed, VTA dopamine neurons are activated when SWR and replay occur during a spatial working memory task, but not during subsequent sleep (Gomperts et al., 2015), indicating close coordination specifically during reward learning.
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to a previous study.

claim: CA1, VTA, and medial prefrontal cortex neurons are jointly coupled via oscillatory mechanisms during spatial working memory.
source: CA1, VTA, and medial prefrontal cortex neurons are jointly coupled via oscillatory mechanisms during spatial working memory (Fujisawa and Buzsáki, 2011), suggesting downstream targets of both replay (Berners-Lee et al., 2021) and VTA dopamine neurons (Lammel et al., 2008) may receive temporally precise conjunctive input from them.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Spatial information is encoded in the firing of hippocampal place cells, which are thought to provide a cognitive map to support memory and navigation.
source: Spatial information is encoded in the firing of hippocampal place cells, which are thought to provide a cognitive map to support memory and navigation (O'Keefe and Dostrovsky, 1971; O'Keefe and Nadel, 1978).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to foundational studies on place cells.

claim: During pauses in locomotion, place cells participate in structured population bursts of activity, representing temporally compressed trajectories through experienced locations, a phenomenon termed replay.
source: During pauses in locomotion, place cells participate in structured population bursts of activity, representing temporally compressed trajectories through experienced locations, a phenomenon termed replay (Diba and Buzsáki, 2007; Foster and Wilson, 2006).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to studies that characterized replay.

claim: Replay sequences can occur in the same order as experience, called forward replay, or in the reverse order of experience, called reverse replay.
source: Replay sequences can occur in the same order as experience, called forward replay, or in the reverse order of experience, called reverse replay (Diba and Buzsáki, 2007; Foster and Wilson, 2006).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to studies that characterized replay directionality.

claim: Replay appears after just one experience in a novel environment.
source: Replay appears after just one experience in a novel environment (Berners-Lee et al., 2022), and is preferentially generated toward goals in goal-directed tasks (Pfeiffer and Foster, 2013; Widloski and Foster, 2022).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Experimentally interrupting or lengthening replay-associated sharp-wave ripples in the local field potential disrupts and enhances learning of a spatial memory task, respectively.
source: Experimentally interrupting or lengthening replay-associated sharp-wave ripples (SWR) in the local field potential (LFP) disrupts and enhances learning of a spatial memory task, respectively (Fernández-Ruiz et al., 2019; Jadhav et al., 2012).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to experimental studies.

claim: Replay is thought to support memory consolidation and online planning.
source: Replay is thus thought to support memory consolidation and online planning (Buzsáki, 2015; Foster, 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to review articles and represents established theory.

claim: Reward drives increased rates of SWR.
source: Intriguingly, reward drives increased rates of SWR (Singer and Frank, 2009), and only reverse replay, not forward, is increased at highly rewarding locations (Ambrose et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Theoretical work suggests replay functions to update spatial representations of value to influence behavior and optimize reward receipt.
source: Theoretical work suggests replay functions to update spatial representations of value to influence behavior and optimize reward receipt (Mattar and Daw, 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to a theoretical study.

claim: Dopamine neuron activity in the ventral tegmental area is consistent with coding of reward prediction error, with increased activity at unexpected rewards and decreased activity with omission of expected rewards.
source: Dopamine neuron activity in the ventral tegmental area (VTA) is consistent with coding of reward prediction error (RPE), with increased activity at unexpected rewards and decreased activity with omission of expected rewards (Schultz et al., 1997).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to a foundational study on dopamine and RPE.

claim: Subsequent work investigated dopamine release in spatial tasks, finding it ramps toward large rewards in a manner consistent with encoding of RPE for a value function over space.
source: Subsequent work investigated dopamine release in spatial tasks, finding it ramps toward large rewards (Guru et al., 2020; Howe et al., 2013) in a manner consistent with encoding of RPE for a value function over space (Kim et al., 2020).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Dopamine release in hippocampus has been implicated in stabilizing place fields.
source: Besides the well-established role of midbrain dopamine neurons in reward processing, dopamine release in hippocampus has been implicated in stabilizing place fields (Kentros et al., 2004), gating the increase in plasticity in dorsal CA1 synapses by novel experiences (Li et al., 2003), and improving memory retention via increasing replay (McNamara et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: VTA activity is increased in novel environments, suggesting the hippocampus and VTA may coordinate to signal spatial novelty and induce learning in new environments.
source: Furthermore, VTA activity is increased in novel environments (Guru et al., 2020; McNamara et al., 2014; Takeuchi et al., 2016), suggesting the hippocampus and VTA may coordinate to signal spatial novelty and induce learning in new environments (Lisman and Grace, 2005).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous studies and represents a theoretical interpretation.

claim: Recent work implicates locus coeruleus as the dominant source of dopaminergic input to dorsal CA1 and show its necessity and sufficiency for novelty-mediated episodic memory consolidation.
source: However, recent work implicates locus coeruleus (LC) as the dominant source of dopaminergic input to dorsal CA1 and show its necessity and sufficiency for novelty-mediated episodic memory consolidation (Kempadoo et al., 2016; Takeuchi et al., 2016), leaving the role of VTA unclear.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to recent studies.

claim: A total of twelve adult male Sprague Dawley TH-cre knock-in rats were used in this experiment, of which seven contributed data to the present report.
source: A total of twelve adult male Sprague Dawley TH-cre knock-in rats (inotiv, HsdSage:SD-THem1(IRES-Cre)Sage, age 3–10 months, 300–750 g) were used in this experiment, of which seven contributed data to the present report.
evidence: This is a direct statement about the experimental subjects.

claim: Two rats were excluded from further analysis due to lack of virus expression evident in post-mortem immunohistochemistry.
source: Two were excluded from further analysis due to lack of virus expression evident in post-mortem immunohistochemistry, two were excluded due to faulty recording hardware, and one was excluded due to non-performance of behavioral tasks.
evidence: This is a direct statement about exclusion criteria.

claim: Rats consistently ran slightly faster toward the Incr. end than the Unch. end in Epoch 2, across all conditions.
source: Rats consistently ran slightly faster toward the Incr. end than the Unch. end in Epoch 2, across all conditions (Figure 1—figure supplement 3).
evidence: This claim is supported by analysis of running velocity data.
